title: Who Said Martial Law?
dek: Seventeen days to the midterms. The president won't rule out an emergency, his friends are saying the quiet part out loud, and Washington's election officials are already drawing up a playbook.
body: Let's get one thing straight before the group chats catch fire. In everything on the record so far, Donald Trump has not said the words 'martial law' about the November 3 midterms. Somebody else did. What the president has said is almost worse, because he said it calmly.
## The friend on the call

On September 30, on a video call for MAGA election activists, Trump's childhood friend and lawyer Peter Ticktin said there would have to be martial law in the event of another rigged election. Axios and Newsweek both reported it on October 16. Ticktin represents Tina Peters, the former Colorado county clerk, who was on the call and met with Trump in October.
> there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election. (Peter Ticktin, Sept. 30)

When The Daily Beast came knocking, Ticktin walked it back to a 'nightmare scenario' in which foreign interests take over voting machines. He has also claimed 'certain coordination' with White House officials, which the White House has not confirmed. Its spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, told Axios the president believes every legal vote must count. She did not say whether he backs emergency powers.
## What the man himself said
On September 28, TIME asked Trump whether he'd rule out declaring a state of emergency before the midterms. His answer, from the published transcript:
> I don't rule anything out or in. We'll see. You mean the Insurrection Act?... I could use it. (Donald Trump to TIME)
He added that a lot of people think he should use it sometimes. Asked about sending ICE agents to polling places, he said he hadn't thought of it.

That's not a one-off. In January he told Reuters that 'we shouldn't even have an election'; the White House said he was joking. In February, on Dan Bongino's podcast, he said Republicans 'ought to nationalize the voting.' Senate Majority Leader John Thune pushed back that it's harder to hack 50 election systems than one, and Speaker Mike Johnson defended state-run elections too.
## The guardrails, such as they are

Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine wrote to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in August that the military has no plans to send forces to polling places or seize election materials. In February, a top DHS election official promised 'no ICE presence at polling locations.' DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has since said agents could show up if there's a threat or a warrant. Arizona's secretary of state said he couldn't take the February promise at face value.

Federal law already makes it a crime to station troops or armed men at a polling place. The Brennan Center argues the Insurrection Act doesn't override that. And courts have been busy: a federal judge in Washington permanently blocked Trump's 2025 election order in a suit brought by Washington and Oregon, and on September 14 the Supreme Court left in place a block on his mail-voting rules for November.
> No federal statute authorizes a president to declare martial law (attorney Jasmine Mines, to Newsweek)
## Meanwhile, in Washington

On September 1, DHS launched what it calls a 'criminal voter fraud surge initiative' in nine states, Washington among them. Two days later, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and Attorney General Nick Brown sent all 39 county election offices a guide covering federal agents at voting sites, subpoenas and warrants, a hypothetical federal seizure of voting equipment, and the Insurrection Act. Brown said there was no reason to believe DHS's inquiry was legitimate.

Washington law limits out-of-state troops coming in without the governor's OK, except where federal law says otherwise. And once a president federalizes the Guard, the governor loses command. Gov. Bob Ferguson said back in June 2025 that Washington would be prepared if Trump tried it here.
## The Sinner's take

Nobody has declared martial law. Nobody in uniform says they're coming. But the president of the United States told a magazine he won't rule an emergency in or out, and his friends are workshopping the phrase on Zoom. That's not a conspiracy theory. That's the transcript.
Washington votes by mail, which is the best defense there is. Fill out your ballot, sign the envelope, and drop it in a county box by 8 p.m. on November 3. Then watch the news like a hawk.

title: "We Turned Our Lights Off"
dek: A father of three died in a burning car after an ICE stop in Michigan. The agent on the 911 call couldn't say what the stop was for. It's the latest name on a list that keeps growing.
body: Sunday morning, September 20, on the southwest side of Grand Rapids, Michigan. ICE agents tried to pull over a car driven by Mario David Coronado Juarez, a Guatemalan construction worker in his 30s who sent money home to his wife, Macedonia, and their three kids. He didn't stop. He drove off, hit a tree, and the car caught fire. He died at the scene.

DHS says its officers immediately dropped the stop and weren't chasing him. They say they saw smoke from about half a mile away and ran back to help and fight the fire before local crews arrived. DHS also says the car was registered to someone else it considered removable.
On October 14, Michigan Public released the 911 call one of the agents made after the crash, obtained through a records request.
> We tried lighting a guy up and he wouldn't stop so we turned our lights off. (ICE agent, 911 call)
When the dispatcher asked what the stop was for, the agent said she'd have to ask her partner.

Grand Rapids police say they had no part in the stop and didn't know about it until the crash. Mayor David LaGrand says it's clear Mario fled from ICE agents, but that a lot of questions remain. He also wrote this: when government agencies cause harm instead of reducing it, they are worse than useless. At the city's request, and at Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's direction, Michigan State Police are investigating. Rep. Hillary Scholten wants to know whether agents had a warrant or any basis for the stop, and has asked ICE to preserve the body-camera and vehicle footage.
> What happened Sunday morning cannot go without justice being served. (Macedonia Juarez, his wife)
## The last fatal shooting

Coronado Juarez died in a crash, not a shooting. The most recent fatal shooting by an immigration agent on record is from July 13 in Biddeford, Maine. An ICE officer shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 25, a Colombian asylum seeker with a pending case and a work permit, on his way to a cleaning job. Bullets hit his 3-year-old daughter's car seat, which the Maine attorney general's office is holding as evidence. ICE says the officer fired fearing for public safety. His partner calls it murder.
## The tally

ABC News counted at least 21 people shot by federal immigration agents in Trump's second term as of late September, eight of them fatally, including three U.S. citizens. Other counts differ. October alone brought two more cases that weren't fatal: an ICE officer fired seven rounds into a car in Manhattan on October 8, hitting the driver in the neck with his 5-year-old son in the back seat, and an ICE SUV ran down a construction worker in Houston on October 10. Harris County's district attorney says that man was intentionally struck and run over. ICE denies it.
Then there are the deaths inside. Twenty-five people have died in ICE detention so far this year, after 31 in 2025. TIME reported in August that detention deaths had hit a 22-year high.
## Here at home

No one in Washington state has died at the hands of immigration agents in 2025 or 2026, as far as the public record shows. A June incident in Blaine left one person injured. But don't get comfortable. As we report elsewhere in this issue, immigration agents are still pulling Washington driver data despite state law.
Know your rights. Keep the hotline numbers in your phone. And if you see ICE, film from a safe distance. In this story, the video and the audio are the only reason we know what we know.
